solution.concept_anchor: Secretary of State for India abolished; functions to Commonwealth Relations Secretary
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students who know the India Office was 'wound up' may conflate this with the functions going to a new 'India and Commonwealth Office' — a plausible-sounding but non-existent entity.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option b — functions did not transfer to the Home Secretary; India's governance was never under the Home Office.
Eliminate option c — there was no 'Secretary of State for India and Commonwealth Affairs' created; this is a plausible fabrication combining real elements.
Eliminate option d — the Foreign Secretary did not absorb India-related functions; foreign affairs and Commonwealth relations were distinct portfolios.

Retain option a — the Secretary of State for India's functions were transferred to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations — correctly reflecting India's new status as a Commonwealth dominion.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places 'Commonwealth Affairs' in the name of a fictional new office (option c) that sounds administratively plausible. Students who know India's new relationship was with the Commonwealth may accept this conflation. The actual recipient of functions was specifically the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations — an existing portfolio that was expanded to absorb India-related functions. The specific name of the portfolio is the knowledge tested.
solution.final_explanation:
The abolition of the Secretary of State for India marked the end of 89 years of direct Whitehall control over India.

• Option (a): Correct. The functions of the Secretary of State for India were transferred to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations. This reflected India's new status as a Dominion within the Commonwealth — no longer a colony requiring a dedicated minister but a partner in a Commonwealth relationship.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The Home Secretary has never been associated with Indian governance; India was never under the Home Office's jurisdiction.
• Option (c): Incorrect. No 'Secretary of State for India and Commonwealth Affairs' was created. This option conflates the abolished India portfolio with the Commonwealth Relations portfolio in a plausible but non-existent hybrid.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Foreign Secretary (Foreign Office) did not absorb India-related functions. Commonwealth relations were treated as distinct from foreign affairs — a distinction Britain maintained until the Foreign and Commonwealth Office merger in 1968.

Value Addition:
• The India Office building in London (now part of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office) still stands as a physical reminder of this era.
• The Commonwealth Relations Office was later merged with the Foreign Office in 1968 to create the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.
• Philip Noel-Baker was the first Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations — a Nobel Peace Prize winner (1959).

solution.concept_anchor: India as successor state; Pakistan as new state under international law

statement_analysis.statement: Under international law, both India and Pakistan were treated as entirely new states, requiring them to apply afresh for United Nations membership and renegotiate all existing treaties of British India.
statement_analysis.reason: India successfully claimed to be the continuing successor state of British India under international law, retaining its UN membership (from 1945), existing treaty obligations, and international legal personality. Pakistan was the new state that required fresh recognition and UN membership.

statement_analysis.statement: India's claim to be the successor state of British India meant that India also inherited the external debts and liabilities of British India, even as Pakistan was deemed a new state not automatically bound by such obligations.
statement_analysis.reason: India's continuity claim had financial implications — it inherited British India's treaty obligations including financial liabilities. Pakistan's new-state status meant it did not automatically inherit these obligations, though subsequent agreements divided the liabilities.

statement_analysis.statement: Pakistan was admitted to the United Nations before India since India had to re-apply as a new state following the dissolution of British India.
statement_analysis.reason: India retained its existing UN membership (British India was a founding UN member from 1945); Pakistan applied separately and was admitted on September 30, 1947. India did not re-apply.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (statement 1 only) tempts students who correctly identify statement 1 as false but also wrongly identify statement 3 as true, missing that both 1 and 3 are incorrect.
elimination_logic: Identify statement 1 as NOT correct — India was treated as the continuing state, not a new state, under international law; it retained UN membership without reapplying.
Identify statement 2 as correct — India's continuity claim carried financial liability implications; this statement is accurate and cannot be the 'not correct' answer.

Identify statement 3 as NOT correct — India retained its existing UN seat; Pakistan (the new state) applied and was admitted in September 1947. The order described in statement 3 is factually reversed.
Both statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap treats India and Pakistan as legally equivalent 'new states' — an error encouraged by the phrase 'two new dominions' in the Independence Act. Under domestic British law, both were new dominions. Under international law, India maintained continuity with British India's legal personality. This asymmetry is conceptually difficult and frequently tested. Statement 3 compounds the trap by implying Pakistan got UN membership first — a reversal that sounds plausible to students who know Pakistan had to apply separately.
solution.final_explanation:
The international law dimension of the 1947 partition creates a significant asymmetry between the two dominions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: India and Pakistan were NOT treated identically under international law. India claimed, and was recognised as, the continuing successor state of British India — retaining its UN membership, existing treaties, and international legal personality. Pakistan was the new state requiring fresh recognition. This is why the statement that 'both required fresh UN applications' is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct: India's continuity claim had implications beyond prestige — it also meant India inherited British India's external debts and liabilities. This was one argument used to justify India's initial reluctance to transfer Pakistan's financial share.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: India retained the existing UN seat; it did not re-apply. Pakistan applied for UN membership and was admitted on September 30, 1947 — after India's continued membership was already established.

Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — option c.

Value Addition:
• British India joined the UN as a founding member in 1945 — despite not being independent, it had separate representation as a distinct political entity.
• The India-Pakistan UN Security Council seat controversy: India retained the existing seat; Pakistan received a General Assembly seat as a new member.
• The precedent of India's continuity influenced the Russia/USSR succession debate in 1991.

solution.concept_anchor: Removal of wartime emergency powers alongside independence grant
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a tempts students who accept both facts as correct and assume the wartime powers being removed caused the constitutional transition described in A, reversing the actual causal direction.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The coming into force of the Independence Act was accompanied by the removal of wartime emergency powers (like the Defence of India Rules), restoring normal constitutional relations between the executive and civil liberties.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Section 9 of the Act did give the Governor-General residual adaptation powers — a limited but real transitional quasi-legislative exception to normal constitutional operation.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The Governor-General's Section 9 adaptation powers are a residual exception, not the mechanism by which wartime emergency powers were removed. The wartime powers lapsed because the emergency legal framework (Defence of India Rules etc.) was no longer applicable in a post-war, post-independence context — this is independent of Section 9. R is a true fact about Section 9 but does not explain why A occurred.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap here involves the student thinking: 'Section 9 adaptation powers caused the removal of wartime emergency powers.' This reverses the relationship. The wartime emergency apparatus was dismantled because the war was over and independence changed the constitutional context — not because Section 9 authorised such adaptation. Section 9 was actually a narrow exception that retained some executive flexibility, not the mechanism for removing the emergency apparatus. Both A and R are true independent facts about the transitional period, but R does not explain A.
solution.final_explanation:
The transitional constitutional moment of 1947 involved both a grant of new powers and a removal of emergency restrictions.

Assertion (A): The transition to independence involved removing the special executive powers accumulated during the war years (Defence of India Rules and similar emergency legislation), fundamentally changing the executive-civil liberties relationship. This is CORRECT — the wartime emergency framework was no longer constitutionally appropriate in independent India.

Reason (R): Section 9 of the Independence Act retained limited adaptation powers for the Governor-General — a quasi-legislative residual authority over existing laws during the transition. This is CORRECT.

However, R does NOT causally explain A. The removal of wartime emergency powers happened because the emergency legal framework was no longer constitutionally appropriate — not because Section 9 authorised adaptation. Section 9 was actually a retaining mechanism (keeping certain executive flexibility) rather than a dismantling mechanism (removing emergency powers). Both facts are true but causally unrelated → option (b).

Value Addition:
• The Defence of India Rules 1939 were the primary wartime emergency instrument — they allowed detention without trial, press censorship, and extensive executive authority.
• Post-independence India retained the Preventive Detention Act 1950 — showing that emergency power instruments did not disappear entirely with independence.
• The emergency provisions in the Indian Constitution (Articles 352-360) created a new, domestically-rooted emergency framework replacing the colonial one.

solution.concept_anchor: Comparative sovereignty — 1947 Act vs. all prior constitutional instruments

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike all previous constitutional instruments governing British India, the Indian Independence Act 1947 explicitly transferred sovereignty rather than merely devolving administrative powers.
statement_analysis.reason: Every prior Act — from the Regulating Act 1773 to the GoI Act 1935 — reformed governance while retaining British parliamentary supremacy. The Independence Act alone effected a categorical transfer of sovereignty, evidenced by the power to repeal the Act itself.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act 1947 was passed at the initiative of the Indian National Congress after negotiations with the British Crown under the terms of the Cripps Mission of 1942.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act was passed by the British Parliament at the initiative of the Labour Government under Clement Attlee. The Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan 1947) was the direct political precursor — not the Cripps Mission of 1942, which was an earlier and failed proposal.

statement_analysis.statement: The Act's provision allowing the Constituent Assembly to repeal or amend the Independence Act itself demonstrates that the British Parliament did not retain any residual legislative supremacy over the new dominions.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 6(4)'s grant of power to repeal the parent Act is the clearest constitutional evidence that Westminster sovereignty did not extend over the new dominions — a complete and unconditional transfer of legislative sovereignty.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act was the shortest Act of the British Parliament ever to have consequences of this magnitude — a contrast frequently noted in constitutional law scholarship.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act is indeed brief — a remarkable contrast to the 321-section Government of India Act 1935 — and this brevity is noted by constitutional scholars as a distinguishing feature of the transfer of sovereignty.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) is deceptive because students who correctly identify statement 2 as false but hesitate on statement 4 (thinking brevity claims need verification) may undercount.
elimination_logic: Confirm statement 1 as correct — the sovereignty transfer argument is well-established and distinguishes the 1947 Act from all predecessors.

Identify statement 2 as incorrect — the Act was a Labour Government initiative under Attlee; the Cripps Mission (1942) was a failed wartime offer, not the direct political precursor. The Mountbatten Plan (June 1947) was the direct antecedent.
Confirm statement 3 as correct — Section 6(4) power to repeal the parent Act is the definitive evidence of unconditional sovereignty transfer.
Confirm statement 4 as correct — the Act's brevity relative to its constitutional consequences is a noted feature in constitutional law literature.
Three statements correct (1, 3, 4) — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial-truth trap: the Cripps Mission is real, negotiations with Britain are real, and the Congress's role in independence is real — but the specific attribution of the Act's initiative to the Cripps Mission is historically wrong. The Cripps Mission failed in 1942; the Act was a 1947 Labour Government initiative flowing from the Mountbatten Plan. Students who know the long arc of independence negotiations may not notice the specific wrong attribution to the Cripps Mission.
solution.final_explanation:
The Independence Act as a culminating instrument involves both its content and its political origins.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The categorical distinction between the 1947 Act and all predecessors is the transfer (not devolution) of sovereignty. Every prior Act from 1773 onwards reformed governance while Westminster retained ultimate supremacy.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Act was initiated by the British Labour Government under Clement Attlee — not at Congress's initiative and not as a consequence of the Cripps Mission. The Cripps Mission (1942) offered Dominion Status after the war as a wartime measure to secure Indian cooperation — it failed. The direct political antecedent of the Act was the Mountbatten Plan of June 3, 1947.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Section 6(4)'s power to repeal the Independence Act itself is the constitutional embodiment of complete sovereignty transfer — Westminster no longer held any residual supremacy.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Independence Act is strikingly brief for its historical significance — a contrast to the 321-section GoI Act 1935, frequently noted in constitutional scholarship.

Three statements correct (1, 3, 4) — option c.

Value Addition:
• The Cripps Mission (March-April 1942) failed partly because it offered post-war Dominion Status, not immediate independence, and excluded defence from Indian control.
• Clement Attlee had been a member of the Simon Commission (1927-30) — giving him direct experience of Indian constitutional questions.
• The Attlee government also passed the Burma Independence Act 1947 and set Ceylon on its path to independence.

solution.concept_anchor: V.P. Menon and Patel as architects of Instrument of Accession

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The Instrument of Accession, through which princely states joined either India or Pakistan, was not a provision of the Indian Independence Act 1947 but was designed as an administrative instrument primarily by V.P. Menon and Sardar Patel.
statement_analysis.reason: The Instrument of Accession was an administrative innovation created outside the Independence Act. V.P. Menon (Secretary of States Ministry) and Sardar Patel (Home Minister) were its principal architects, filling the legal vacuum created by the lapse of paramountcy under Section 7 of the Act.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Under the initial Instrument of Accession, princely states that signed the document surrendered complete sovereignty over all matters of governance to the dominion they joined, retaining no autonomous powers whatsoever.
statement_analysis.reason: The initial Instrument of Accession covered only three subjects — Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. States retained internal autonomy over all other matters. Full merger was a subsequent and separate process for many states.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect) is the answer — but option a tests whether students mistakenly think both are wrong. Wait, re-checking the option mapping for two-statement-relationship: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) S1 correct S2 incorrect, (d) S1 incorrect S2 correct. Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option c. Correcting.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — The Instrument of Accession was designed by V.P. Menon and Patel outside the Act's statutory provisions; this is historically accurate. Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2 — The initial Instrument covered only Defence, External Affairs, and Communications; internal autonomy was retained. Full surrender of sovereignty came through separate merger agreements. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the assumption that 'accession' meant complete merger — a common misconception. The initial Instrument was deliberately limited to three subjects to make it politically acceptable to princely states. Hyderabad and Kashmir's complications partly arose because these distinctions (accession vs. full merger) were legally real. Students who think signing the Instrument meant instant complete absorption into India will accept Statement 2 as correct, leading to option a (both correct) as the wrong choice.
solution.final_explanation:
The Instrument of Accession is often misunderstood as automatically complete integration — it was not.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Instrument of Accession was not statutory — it was not found in the text of the Independence Act. V.P. Menon (who had also helped draft the Mountbatten Plan) and Sardar Patel created it as an administrative solution to the legal vacuum created by Section 7. This is a critical distinction for UPSC.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The initial Instrument of Accession covered only three subjects: Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. States retained extensive internal autonomy in all other areas. Complete merger into India came through separate and subsequent Merger Agreements — a different and more comprehensive instrument. Jammu & Kashmir's Instrument of Accession, for instance, specifically limited accession to these three subjects, which became the basis of later debates about special status.

Correct answer: (c) — Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The States Ministry, under Patel and Menon, secured accession of most states before August 15, 1947 — a remarkable administrative achievement.
• The Merger Agreement (different from the Instrument of Accession) transferred administrative control; many states signed this between 1947 and 1949.
• Travancore and Jodhpur were among the states that initially hesitated but were persuaded before August 15, 1947.

solution.concept_anchor: Provincial accession mechanisms — referendum vs. legislature vote vs. partition
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because it correctly places Sylhet with the referendum but swaps the mechanisms for Punjab and NWFP, exploiting the confusion between 'referendum' (NWFP) and 'boundary commission' (Punjab).
elimination_logic: Confirm A — Punjab was one of the two internally partitioned provinces; it required a Boundary Commission — matched with List II item 3.
Confirm B — Sylhet's referendum is the only one directly mandated by the Independence Act — matched with List II item 1.
Identify C — NWFP joined Pakistan through a referendum under the 3 June Plan framework, not a Boundary Commission (which would imply internal partition) — matched with List II item 2.

Identify D — British Baluchistan was handled through the Shahi Jirga and Quetta municipality, not a standard provincial legislature vote — matched with List II item 4. Full matching: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 = option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap involves the confusion between NWFP's referendum and the 3 June Plan basis. Students often conflate 'NWFP had a referendum' with 'NWFP was partitioned like Punjab' — conflating the mechanism (referendum) with the outcome (partition). NWFP was not internally divided; it went entirely to Pakistan based on its referendum result. British Baluchistan's unique mechanism (Shahi Jirga) is the most often missed detail — students default to 'referendum' or 'legislature vote' for all provinces.
solution.final_explanation:
Each province had a distinct mechanism for determining its fate — these distinctions are a rich source of UPSC questions.

Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 (Option c)

• A (Punjab) → 3 (Internal partition with a separate Boundary Commission under Radcliffe): Punjab was divided into West Punjab (Pakistan) and East Punjab (India) — one of two provinces internally partitioned.
• B (Sylhet, Assam) → 1 (Referendum directly mandated within the Indian Independence Act 1947): The Sylhet referendum is the only plebiscite specifically provided for in the Act's text. Sylhet voted to join East Pakistan.
• C (North-West Frontier Province) → 2 (Referendum conducted under the 3 June Plan framework, not directly mandated by the Act): NWFP's referendum was a 3 June Plan mechanism — the Act gave it legal force but did not directly mandate it. NWFP went entirely to Pakistan.
• D (British Baluchistan) → 4 (Accession through the Shahi Jirga and Quetta municipality — a unique mechanism not applicable to standard provinces): British Baluchistan was a Chief Commissioner's Province with tribal areas, requiring a specially constituted mechanism.

Value Addition:
• The NWFP referendum was boycotted by the Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan faction — the Congress-affiliated 'Frontier Gandhi' who opposed joining Pakistan.
• West Punjab and East Punjab were announced in the Radcliffe Award on August 17, 1947.
• British Baluchistan's accession was among the most complex — tribal areas had a different legal status from administered territories.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence: Cabinet Mission → 3 June Plan → Royal Assent → appointed date
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because placing the 3 June Plan after Royal Assent suggests the political agreement preceded the legal instrument — students may invert the two because they know the Mountbatten Plan led to the Act but cannot place their dates precisely.
elimination_logic: Establish Q: The Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946) precedes all others — it set up the Constituent Assembly and was the constitutional starting point.
Establish P: The Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) was announced on June 3, 1947 — after the Cabinet Mission but before the Act.
Establish R: Royal Assent to the Independence Act was on July 18, 1947 — after the political plan but before the appointed date.
Establish S: The appointed date (August 15, 1947) is the last in sequence — when the Act came into operational effect. Order: Q → P → R → S = option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap involves candidates who know the general sequence but cannot place exact dates — specifically, they may place Royal Assent (July 18) before the 3 June Plan (June 3) or merge the two political and legal instruments in the wrong order. The Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946) is often forgotten as the starting constitutional point because students focus on 1947 events, neglecting that the Constituent Assembly — which the Independence Act empowered — was actually constituted over a year before independence.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional sequence leading to independence involves both political agreements and legal instruments, each with distinct dates.

Correct order: Q → P → R → S (Option b)

• Q (Cabinet Mission Plan, May 1946): The constitutional starting point for the final independence process. It proposed the Constituent Assembly and a united India framework. Though the federal plan failed, it set the institutional machinery in motion.
• P (Mountbatten Plan / 3 June Plan, June 3, 1947): The political agreement specifying partition of British India into two dominions, partition of Punjab and Bengal, and mechanisms for provincial decisions.
• R (Royal Assent to the Indian Independence Act, July 18, 1947): The Act received Royal Assent nearly six weeks after the Mountbatten Plan, converting the political agreement into a legal instrument.
• S (Appointed date — dominions come into existence, August 15, 1947): The operational effect date when both dominions formally came into legal existence.

Value Addition:
• The Cabinet Mission had three members: Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander.
• The 3 June Plan was announced simultaneously in London (by Attlee) and Delhi (by Mountbatten) — a carefully coordinated political communication.
• The gap between Royal Assent (July 18) and the appointed date (August 15) was deliberately kept at less than a month to minimise the period of uncertainty.

solution.concept_anchor: Features of the Independence Act — what it explicitly provided for
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because provisions for a joint constituent assembly sounds constitutionally plausible — students who know the Constituent Assembly existed may think a joint body was an early proposal under the Act.
elimination_logic: Options a, c, and d are all genuine features of the Independence Act: protection of civil service contractual rights (a), each dominion having its own Constituent Assembly with sovereign powers (c and d are related to this).

Wait — re-examining: (a) protection of ICS contractual rights — genuine; (b) establishment of a joint constituent assembly for both dominions — fabricated; (c) Section 9 adaptation powers for Governor-General — genuine; (d) lapse of paramountcy over princely states — genuine.
Option b is the odd one out — a joint constituent assembly was not provided for; each dominion had its own separate Constituent Assembly.
Confirm: the Independence Act explicitly provided for separate Constituent Assemblies, not a joint one — option b is the plausible fabrication.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b exploits the plausible-fabrication mechanism — 'a joint constituent assembly' sounds reasonable to a student who knows that before partition, the Cabinet Mission Plan had proposed a joint (united India) constitutional process. The confusion between the Cabinet Mission's proposed joint framework and the Independence Act's separate-assembly approach is the trap. The Act definitively separated the two assemblies; there was no joint body under the Act.
solution.final_explanation:
The Independence Act explicitly made several specific provisions — identifying what it did NOT provide is an important precision skill.

• Option (a): Genuine provision. The Act protected the contractual rights of existing civil servants, including ICS officers, ensuring compensation and pension rights for British officers who chose not to serve the new dominions — essential for administrative continuity.
• Option (b): This is the odd one out — a plausible fabrication. The Act did NOT establish a joint constituent assembly for both dominions. Each dominion had its own separate Constituent Assembly. The idea of a joint assembly belonged to the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), which proposed a united India approach. Partition ended this possibility; the Independence Act created two entirely separate constitutional bodies.
• Option (c): Genuine provision. Section 9 specifically gave the Governor-General of each dominion the power to adapt and modify existing laws during the transitional period.
• Option (d): Genuine provision. Section 7 of the Act caused the lapse of British paramountcy over princely states — one of its most consequential provisions.

Value Addition:
• The Cabinet Mission's proposed 'Union Constituent Assembly' was designed to frame a constitution for a united India; partition made this impossible.
• Each dominion's Constituent Assembly had a different membership — India's had representatives from the remaining Indian provinces and states; Pakistan's had members from the Pakistani provinces.
• Pakistan's Constituent Assembly took nine years to produce a constitution (1956) — India's took two years and eleven months (November 1949 adoption).

solution.concept_anchor: Section 6(4) sovereignty and India's Republic transition without further British legislation

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act 1947 required India to obtain fresh legislation from the British Parliament in order to become a Republic in 1950.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 6(4) of the Act gave the Constituent Assembly power to repeal or amend the Act itself — this is precisely why India could become a Republic in 1950 without requiring any further Act of Westminster. The sovereignty transfer was complete and unconditional.

statement_analysis.statement: The power granted to the Constituent Assembly by the Independence Act to frame any constitution included the power to establish a Republic that severed formal ties with the Crown.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act's grant of sovereign constitution-making power was unlimited — it explicitly allowed the Constituent Assembly to frame any constitution it chose, including a republican one, without requiring British parliamentary approval.

statement_analysis.statement: India's becoming a Republic in 1950 while remaining within the Commonwealth required a separate political agreement among Commonwealth members — the Independence Act alone was insufficient to settle this.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Independence Act gave India the legal power to become a Republic, remaining in the Commonwealth as a Republic required a new constitutional formula — this was provided by the London Declaration of April 1949, which recognised the King as a symbol of free association, not a constitutional head.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (statement 2 only) tempts students who accept statement 2 but are unsure whether statement 3 is accurate, doubting whether a separate political agreement (London Declaration) was really needed or whether the Act was self-sufficient for Commonwealth membership.
elimination_logic: Eliminate statement 1 as incorrect — Section 6(4) explicitly gave the power to repeal the parent Act itself; India did not need further Westminster legislation to become a Republic.
Confirm statement 2 as correct — the unconditional sovereignty transfer included the power to frame a republican constitution.

Confirm statement 3 as correct — the Act gave legal power for republican status, but Commonwealth membership as a Republic required the London Declaration 1949 — a political agreement, not legislation.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the scope-extension mechanism — students may think 'becoming a Republic requires additional British legislation because the Act only granted dominion status.' This misunderstands the scope of Section 6(4). The Act's sovereignty transfer was unconditional — India needed no further Westminster approval. Statement 3, however, is also correct but for a different reason: the Commonwealth membership question (as opposed to the domestic constitutional question) did require a new political formula, not more legislation. This two-layer distinction — legal power vs. political arrangement — is the sophisticated element of this question.
solution.final_explanation:
India's transition from Dominion to Republic involved two separate tracks — the domestic constitutional track and the Commonwealth membership track.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Independence Act's Section 6(4) gave India's Constituent Assembly full power to repeal or amend the Act and frame any constitution it chose. India did not require any further Act of the British Parliament to become a Republic on January 26, 1950. The sovereignty transfer was complete and required no further Westminster involvement.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The power to frame any constitution — including a republican one with no Crown connection — was explicitly included in the sovereignty transfer. This is the legal basis for India's becoming a Republic without British approval.
• Statement 3 — Correct but on a different ground: While India could legally become a Republic without Westminster's involvement (domestic constitutional power), remaining within the Commonwealth as a Republic required a new political formula. The London Declaration of April 1949 — agreed at a Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference — created the model of a Republic acknowledging the King as a 'symbol of free association' of Commonwealth members. Without this political agreement, India would have had to leave the Commonwealth upon becoming a Republic.

Statements 2 and 3 correct — option d.

Value Addition:
• The London Declaration (1949) is constitutionally significant — it divorced Commonwealth membership from shared allegiance to the Crown.
• India was the first Republic to remain within the Commonwealth — a model subsequently followed by many newly independent nations.
• Pakistan became a Republic in 1956 and left the Commonwealth in 1972 (rejoining in 1989).

solution.concept_anchor: Jinnah as GG of Pakistan — constitutional significance of political leader as GG
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because Mountbatten's prior role as Viceroy of both territories makes students assume he would naturally continue as Governor-General for both — a logical but factually incorrect extension.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option d — the Independence Act specifically allowed each dominion to have its own Governor-General; a single shared GG for both was not required.

Eliminate option c — while Mountbatten continued as GG of India, Jinnah chose to be his own GG for Pakistan; the same person serving both simultaneously was rejected by Pakistan's own constitutional choice.
Eliminate option b — the King was the constitutional head through the GGs, not through a shared representative body; the Governor-General was the King's representative in each dominion separately.

Retain option a — the correct application: the Act permitted each dominion to appoint its own GG independently. Jinnah exercised this right by appointing himself as Pakistan's GG — a choice that had no precedent in Commonwealth constitutional practice and concentrated executive and political power in one person.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap is the assumption that Mountbatten served both dominions as Governor-General. This is a natural error because Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of both territories. Students who project the Viceroy's unified role onto the post-partition GG role will choose option c. The crucial fact is that Pakistan's constitutional choice — having Jinnah as its own GG — was a deliberate and consequential decision under the Act's provision for separate Governors-General.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario tests the Governor-General provisions of the Independence Act applied to a real constitutional choice.

The applicable provision: The Independence Act allowed each dominion to have its own Governor-General appointed independently. This provision was exercised differently by the two dominions.

• Option (a): Correct. The Act permitted each dominion to appoint its own Governor-General. India chose Mountbatten; Pakistan chose Jinnah himself. This was constitutionally permissible under the Act's design. Jinnah's decision concentrated political leadership and symbolic constitutional authority in one person — an unprecedented Commonwealth choice.
• Option (b): Incorrect. There was no provision for a shared Commonwealth representative body acting as constitutional head of both dominions simultaneously. The King was represented separately in each dominion through that dominion's own Governor-General.
• Option (c): Incorrect. While Mountbatten served as GG of India (not of both), this was because Jinnah chose to become Pakistan's own GG — not because the Act prohibited a shared arrangement. The Act allowed separate GGs; Pakistan exercised this provision decisively.
• Option (d): Incorrect. A single GG serving both dominions was not required by the Act — each dominion's GG was appointed independently, representing the Crown's separate constitutional relationship with each.

Value Addition:
• Jinnah's tenure as GG of Pakistan lasted only until his death in September 1948 — just over a year after independence.
• Mountbatten's GG tenure in India ended in June 1948; C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) succeeded him.
• The practice of a political leader also serving as GG has been criticised as destabilising — it removed the constitutional check that a separate GG provides.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 7 paramountcy lapse — practical vs. legal sovereignty of states

statement_analysis.statement: Section 7 of the Indian Independence Act 1947 caused the lapse of British paramountcy, theoretically making each princely state a sovereign entity on August 15, 1947.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 7 explicitly terminated British suzerainty over princely states; legally, each state became a sovereign entity on the appointed date, though this sovereignty was practically unsustainable for most states.

statement_analysis.statement: The lapse of paramountcy under the Independence Act automatically merged all princely states into the Dominion of India by operation of law.
statement_analysis.reason: Paramountcy lapsed, but no automatic merger occurred. Each state's accession required a separate Instrument of Accession — a voluntary (or coerced) political act. The legal vacuum between lapse and accession is precisely why states like Hyderabad and Junagadh caused crises.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'independence' of princely states following the lapse of paramountcy, though legally real under the Act, was politically untenable for most states due to geographic, economic, and military factors.
statement_analysis.reason: The legal position (sovereignty from August 15) and the practical position (surrounded by one dominion or the other, with no military capability, and economically integrated with British India) were in stark conflict — the 'independence' was real in law but unviable in fact.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (statements 1 and 2) is the strongest distractor because students who correctly identify statement 1 as true may also incorrectly accept statement 2, confusing 'paramountcy lapsed' with 'merger happened.'
elimination_logic: Confirm statement 1 as correct — Section 7's effect of creating theoretical sovereignty for princely states is a documented provision of the Act.

Eliminate statement 2 as incorrect — the lapse of paramountcy created a legal vacuum, not automatic merger. Merger required separate Instruments of Accession; states like Hyderabad exploited the vacuum to resist accession.
Confirm statement 3 as correct — the distinction between legal sovereignty and practical viability of independence is a well-documented aspect of the partition period.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the scope-extension trap — it extends the effect of Section 7 beyond what the Act actually provides. 'Paramountcy lapsed' is converted to 'automatic merger occurred' — a logical but legally incorrect extension. Students who have a general understanding that 'princely states joined India' may not distinguish between the legal mechanism (separate Instruments of Accession) and the legal effect of Section 7 (only paramountcy lapse, not merger). The entire Hyderabad and Junagadh crisis makes sense only if one understands that Section 7 created a vacuum rather than mandating merger.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 7 of the Independence Act is one of the most consequential and misunderstood provisions in Indian constitutional history.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 7 explicitly terminated British paramountcy (suzerainty) over princely states with effect from August 15, 1947. Legally, each state became sovereign. This was not mere political rhetoric — it had genuine legal consequences, as the Hyderabad and Junagadh cases demonstrated.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No automatic merger occurred under the Act. The lapse of paramountcy created a legal vacuum — states were sovereign but unattached. Accession required a separate voluntary legal act (the Instrument of Accession) by each ruler. States that refused (Hyderabad, Junagadh, Kashmir initially) were not automatically part of India by operation of law.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The disconnect between legal sovereignty (real under the Act) and practical independence (impossible for landlocked states surrounded by India, economically integrated with British India, and militarily weak) is the key to understanding why 562 states ultimately joined India or Pakistan. Legal reality and political viability pointed in opposite directions.

Statements 1 and 3 correct — option c.

Value Addition:
• Hyderabad's Nizam was the richest man in the world at the time — yet his state's 'independence' was ended by military action (Operation Polo) within 13 months.
• Junagadh, despite being on the Kathiawar peninsula (geographically part of India's territory), initially attempted to accede to Pakistan — illustrating the legal vacuum's political dangers.
• The integration of 562 princely states was largely complete by 1950 — one of the most remarkable political integrations in modern history.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act 1947 explicitly specified the 17.5% share of financial assets to be allocated to Pakistan in its statutory provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: The 17.5% financial allocation for Pakistan was determined through separate inter-dominion administrative negotiations, not specified within the text of the Independence Act itself. The Act provided the legal framework for division, not the specific ratios.

statement_analysis.statement: The Act protected the pension and service rights of British Indian Army officers who chose to retire rather than serve either of the new dominions.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act's civil service continuity provisions extended to military officers — those who chose not to serve were entitled to compensation and pension protection, ensuring orderly military transition rather than mass resignation.

statement_analysis.statement: The actual division of the British Indian Army between India and Pakistan was supervised by a transitional body known as the Joint Defence Council, which was established separately from the Independence Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Joint Defence Council, with Field Marshal Sir Claude Auchinleck as Supreme Commander, supervised the military transition. It was established through separate administrative arrangements, not as a statutory body under the Independence Act.

statement_analysis.statement: The Independence Act's provisions on asset division were self-executing — no further negotiation between the two dominions was required to implement the division of financial and military assets.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act provided only the legal authority and framework for division; extensive subsequent negotiation, dispute, and administrative arrangement were required. India's initial withholding of Pakistan's financial share demonstrates the Act's provisions were not self-executing.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) misleads students who accept statement 1 (the 17.5% figure being 'in the Act') and therefore think three statements are correct rather than two.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect — the 17.5% ratio was negotiated separately, not specified in the Act.
Statement 2 is correct — service protection provisions applied to military as well as civilian officers.
Statement 3 is correct — the Joint Defence Council was a separate administrative body, not a statutory creation of the Act.
Statement 4 is incorrect — the Act's provisions were framework-level, not self-executing; subsequent negotiations were essential.
Two statements (2 and 3) are correct — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the most seductive distractor — the 17.5% figure is a well-known fact about partition and students who have encountered it assume it was in the Act. The Act authorised division; the specific ratio was an administrative outcome of negotiations. Statement 4 compounds this by making a 'self-executing' claim that sounds plausible for a statutory instrument. The partial-truth here is that the Act did provide for division — it just did not specify how, in what ratio, and with what mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
The Independence Act's role in dividing military and financial assets must be distinguished from the actual administrative process of division.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 17.5% financial allocation to Pakistan is a well-known partition fact, but it was determined through negotiation — not inscribed in the Act. The Act authorised the legal framework for asset division; ratios were determined through a separate partition council process.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Act's civil service and administrative continuity provisions protected not just civilian ICS officers but also military officers. Those who chose not to serve were entitled to compensation and pension rights.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Joint Defence Council, under Field Marshal Sir Claude Auchinleck, was established as a transitional supervisory body for military division. It was not a statutory creation of the Independence Act — it was a separately constituted administrative body.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Act was a framework instrument; it was emphatically not self-executing. The controversy over Pakistan's financial share — which Gandhi's fast partly sought to resolve — demonstrates that the Act's authority alone was insufficient without political will and separate administrative arrangements.

Two statements (2 and 3) correct — option b.

Value Addition:
• Gandhi's fast in January 1948 was partly to pressure India to release Pakistan's Rs. 55 crore financial share — linking a constitutional matter with a moral one.
• The partition of military assets took months; some units were fighting on both sides' behalf simultaneously during the early Kashmir conflict.
• India received the larger share of armaments partly due to its greater geographic extent and the location of most military installations.

elimination_logic: Eliminate option a — Burma and the Indian Independence Act: Burma's independence (January 4, 1948) was governed by the Burma Independence Act 1947 — a separate Act. This pair attributes it incorrectly to the Indian Independence Act.

Eliminate option b — Ceylon and Commonwealth membership: Ceylon did join the Commonwealth upon independence in February 1948; the pair correctly identifies this but is this the correctly matched pair asked? The stem asks which pair is CORRECTLY matched — Ceylon joined Commonwealth, so this would be correct. Wait, re-reading: option b says 'Ceylon achieved independence in 1948 under the Indian Independence Act 1947' — this is the pairing being evaluated. Let me re-examine all options.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap groups Burma, Ceylon, India, and Pakistan as part of one decolonization event. Students who know all four became independent around the same time may assume they were governed by the same Act. Burma's independence was under the Burma Independence Act 1947 (separate legislation) and it made the specific choice to remain outside the Commonwealth — a distinctive fact that separates it from India, Pakistan, and Ceylon. Students who have not specifically studied Burma's post-independence Commonwealth status will not identify option d as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing the independence instruments and post-independence Commonwealth choices of South and Southeast Asian nations is a frequently tested precision area.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. Burma's independence (January 4, 1948) was not governed by the Indian Independence Act 1947. Burma had its own separate Burma Independence Act 1947 — distinct legislation, distinct date, distinct constitutional outcome.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Ceylon's independence was achieved under the Ceylon Independence Act 1947, which came into force on February 4, 1948. The Indian Independence Act 1947 had no application to Ceylon.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Both India and Pakistan were new dominions under domestic British law (the Independence Act), but under international law India claimed successor-state continuity while Pakistan was the new state. This option reverses the positions.
• Option (d): Correctly matched. Burma, upon achieving independence in January 1948 under the Burma Independence Act, specifically chose NOT to join the Commonwealth of Nations — a deliberate choice distinguishing it from India, Pakistan, and Ceylon, which all remained Commonwealth members (at least initially).

Value Addition:
• Burma's decision to stay outside the Commonwealth reflected its desire for complete non-alignment and rejection of any residual British institutional connection.
• Burma (now Myanmar) has never rejoined the Commonwealth — a consistent position maintained since 1948.
• Ceylon became a Republic in 1972, renamed itself Sri Lanka, and remains in the Commonwealth today.
